title: 'A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho'
summary: The road in the parable drops about a kilometre in vertical height over some 27 km of bare limestone gorge. 'Down' describes the ground.
body: Jericho sits at roughly 250 m below sea level, the lowest city on earth. Jerusalem stands at about 750 m above it. The Roman-period road between them ran some 27 km through the Judean wilderness, climbing about 1,000 m — an average gradient near 4%, with much steeper stretches. Luke's 'going down' and 'going up' (Luke 10:30; 19:28) are simple description.

The route threads the head of the Wadi Qelt, a narrow limestone gorge with blind bends and high sides. Joshua 18:17 names the ascent of Adummim, the red ascent. Josephus describes the descent to Jericho as rugged and desolate.

The Babylonian Talmud records that when each of the twenty-four priestly watches went up for its week of temple service, 'half the priestly watch would ascend from all over Eretz Yisrael to Jerusalem, and half the priestly watch would ascend from Jericho' (Taanit 27a). The parable's first two travellers are a priest and a Levite.
The elevations are modern survey figures and the road length depends on which line you trace; both are given here as approximations.

title: Why the Sea of Galilee turns violent so fast
summary: A warm lake 210 m below sea level, ringed by cold highlands 700 to 2,800 m above it, with wind funnelled down steep ravines. Sudden squalls are part of the lake's weather.
body: The lake is small: about 21 km long, 13 km wide, 43 m deep at most. Its surface sits roughly 210 m below sea level, in a rift valley. To the east the Golan plateau rises to more than 700 m within a few kilometres of the shore; to the north-east Mount Hermon reaches 2,814 m.

The lake surface holds warm, humid air. When cold, dry air off those uplands spills over the rim — most often on an easterly — it is denser, so it drops through the ravines and wadis and spreads across the water while the warm air is forced up. The narrow valleys funnel and accelerate it. The result is a squall that arrives with little warning over open water and can raise steep short waves within half an hour, in a boat with a metre of freeboard.
The Gospels tell of more than one storm on the lake. In Mark 4:39 what stops is both the wind and the waves.
The physical measurements are survey data. The description of the mechanism is a general account of the basin, not a measurement of any particular storm.

title: Gehenna is a valley, and the rubbish-dump story is medieval
summary: The word behind 'hell' in the Gospels is Ge-Hinnom, a real ravine on the south-west side of Jerusalem. The explanation that it was a perpetually burning garbage dump goes back, Lloyd Bailey found, to a rabbi writing about AD 1200, with no earlier evidence for it.
body: Gehenna transliterates the Aramaic Ge-Hinnam, from Hebrew Ge ben-Hinnom, 'the valley of the son of Hinnom'. It is a specific place: the ravine curving round the south and west of the Old City, meeting the Kidron below the City of David. In Joshua 15:8 and 18:16 it is simply a boundary marker.

What made the name terrible is what happened there. 2 Kings 23:10 says Josiah defiled Topheth 'which is in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, so that no one could make his son or his daughter pass through the fire to Molech'; 2 Chronicles 28:3 and 33:6 name Ahaz and Manasseh as kings who did. Jeremiah 7:31-32 and 19:6 pronounce that the place will be renamed the Valley of Slaughter and used as a burial ground until there is no room left. By the intertestamental period (1 Enoch 27, 90) the valley's name had become the name of the place of final judgement, and that is how the Gospels use it.

Lloyd Bailey (1986) looked for the dump in the ancient sources and found no reference in the Hebrew Bible, the Apocrypha, Josephus, the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Mishnah or the Talmud to Jerusalem's refuse being burned in the Hinnom valley, and no archaeological deposit of the kind identified there. The earliest statement of it he found is in Rabbi David Kimhi's commentary on Psalm 27, written around AD 1200, more than a millennium after the Gospels.

title: You always go up to Jerusalem
summary: Scripture speaks of going up to Jerusalem and down from it regardless of the compass direction — from Galilee in the north, from Jericho in the east, from Egypt in the south. The city stands on a ridge.
body: Jerusalem sits on the central hill country at roughly 750 m above sea level, with ground falling away on three sides: to the Jordan rift in the east, the Shephelah and coastal plain in the west, and the desert in the south. Every approach is a climb. So Galileans travelling south 'go up' (Luke 2:42), Paul returning from Antioch in the north 'goes up' (Acts 15:2), and the good Samaritan's traveller heading east and downhill 'goes down' (Luke 10:30).

The Hebrew verb alah, 'go up', became the technical term for pilgrimage; the three pilgrim feasts are the regalim, and the noun aliyah, 'a going up', is still the ordinary Hebrew word for immigrating to the land and for being called up to read the Torah.

Psalms 120-134 carry the heading shir hammaalot, 'a song of ascents'. The Mishnah sets the Levites with their instruments on the fifteen steps between the temple's courts, 'corresponding to the fifteen Songs of the Ascents' (Sukkah 5:4). The heading has also been read as pilgrims' songs on the way up, or as a poetic device in which each verse steps up from the last.

title: Joel's locusts, photographed in 1915
summary: In spring 1915 a locust plague stripped Palestine. Photographers of Jerusalem's American Colony recorded it stage by stage: the swarms, the crawling young, and the trees left bare.
body: Joel names four kinds of locust (1:4, 2:25). They have been read as four species and as stages of one insect's growth. In a plague, adults lay eggs, and the young that hatch, wingless and crawling, eat what the swarm left before they can fly; the 1915 photographers called the crawling stage 'most destructive'.

The American Colony photographers titled their series 'The terrible plague of locusts in Palestine, March–June 1915'. It shows masses of locusts on an olive tree, locusts devouring palm leaves, storks in pursuit of the swarm, and the Garden of Gethsemane before and after.

Joel 1:7 says the swarm 'has stripped off the bark … the branches have turned white', and 2:7-9 that the locusts 'scale the walls', 'run along the wall' and 'climb into houses, entering through windows like thieves'. The photographs show trees stripped bare. Joel 2:10 says the sun and moon grow dark; whether that describes a swarm thick enough to block the light, or more, the verse does not say.
